name: Legionarii Mattiarii seniores (palatina)

abilities.name: Testudo
abilities.text: The troops of this unit raise their shields above their heads in a defensive formation.

abilities.name: Square
abilities.text: The unit moves into a close square formation. Note that it cannot move whilst this ability is active.

abilities.name: Shield Wall
abilities.text: The unit moves into a close formation and raises shields.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Formation Attack
attributes.text: The unit will try to stay in formation when in melee.

attributes.name: Hide (forest)
attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: The name Mattiarii probably comes from the name of the lead throwing darts mattiobarbuli (Vegetius 1.17), also known as martiobarbuli, which can be translated as «little barbs of Mars» or «small darts of Mars». They are also called plumbatae (plumbatae means the «lead-weighted»). The main weapon of the Mattiarii was probably the plumbatae, small throwing darts weighted with the lead pommel. A pattern of their shield is shown in many manuscripts of the Notitia Dignitatum, but the name of the unit is almost always recorded as simply Matiarii, probably a normal simplification for that time. Mattiarii appear frequently in many sources, not only in Ammianus Marcellinus, but also, for example, in a fragment of Eutychianus of Cappadocia (FGH IV,6), quoted by Malalas, a 6th century Byzantine chronicler who wrote about Julian's Persian campaign. According to historians R. Scharf and E.A. Mekhamadiev, the terms seniores and iuniores reflected the process of gradual division of the late Roman legions, when from the ranks of the older legions, designated as seniores, were separated new units called iuniores. The formation of iuniores units allowed the sons of soldiers to begin their service in the same privileged military units in which their fathers (seniores) had served, and to advance up the military ranks relatively quickly.
history: Exculcatores' were ranged infantry units that operated as part of the Auxilia Palatina - Legions of auxiliaries created during Constantine the Great's military reforms of the early 4th century AD. They were formed of local troops, and often took the names of the tribes from which they were drafted. As auxiliaries, it is safe to assume that exculcatores operated along the frontiers, stationed in Gaul or Britannia. Although there is reference to their acting as standard javelinmen, the Notitia Dignitatum contains some evidence that exculcatores were specialist units, used for tracking in conjunction with another scouting corps known as 'exploratores'.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
